title: Consider Carefully Your Ways
subtitle: Haggai 1
description: Sixteen years home, God's house still in ruins, and a prophet sent to audit a pierced bag.
paragraphs: The word arrived with a date on it, the first of many in this short book. “In the second year of the reign of Darius, on the first day of the sixth month, the word of the LORD came through Haggai the prophet to Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah, and to Joshua son of Jehozadak, the high priest.” Sixteen years had passed since Cyrus let the exiles go home. The foundation of God's house had been laid in Jerusalem and then left, year after year, while the returned people built their own lives around the ruin. Haggai opens by quoting the people's own settled conclusion back to them, in God's voice: these people say the time has not yet come to rebuild the house of the LORD. The whole book is the argument with that sentence.

The counter-question is the most domestic charge in all the prophets. “Is it a time for you yourselves to live in your paneled houses, while this house lies in ruins?” Paneled houses are finished houses, roofed and lined, the kind you build when you plan to stay. God's house had a foundation and weather. Then comes the command the book will repeat until it echoes, twice in this chapter alone: “Consider carefully your ways.” What follows is not a sermon about the temple at all. It is an audit of their ordinary lives, five clauses of almost-but-never-enough: “You have planted much but harvested little. You eat but never have enough. You drink but never have your fill. You put on clothes but never get warm. You earn wages to put into a bag pierced through.”

Notice what the audit does not say. It does not say they plant nothing, eat nothing, earn nothing. They work, and the work almost feeds them, and the gap between the planting and the harvest is exactly the size of the unfinished house. The command comes again, “Consider carefully your ways,” and this time it comes with a work order attached: “Go up into the hills, bring down lumber, and build the house, so that I may take pleasure in it and be glorified, says the LORD.” Hills, lumber, building. The remedy for sixteen years of theological postponement is a trip to the timberline.

Then God does His own considering out loud, and names Himself as the author of the lean years. “You expected much, but behold, it amounted to little. And what you brought home, I blew away. Why? declares the LORD of Hosts. Because My house still lies in ruins, while each of you is busy with his own house.” The blowing away is deliberate and so is the drought that follows it in the text: “Therefore, on account of you the heavens have withheld their dew and the earth has withheld its crops.” The heavens withholding and the earth withholding are not weather in this oracle. They are a summons with the subpoena spelled out.

“I have summoned a drought on the fields and on the mountains, on the grain, new wine, and oil, and on whatever the ground yields, on man and beast, and on all the labor of your hands.” The first oracle ends there, on the drought's full inventory, with no response recorded yet. The word came on the first day of the sixth month. What the governor, the priest, and the remnant did about a summons like that, and how long heaven left them to think it over, is the next thing the little book records, and it records it with the same care for dates it has shown from its first line.

title: I Am with You
subtitle: Haggai 1
description: One sermon, three weeks of considering, and the work begins on the twenty-fourth day.
paragraphs: The response, when the book records it, names every party the oracle named and adds the one party the oracle was about. “Then Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and Joshua son of Jehozadak, the high priest, as well as all the remnant of the people, obeyed the voice of the LORD their God and the words of the prophet Haggai, because the LORD their God had sent him. So the people feared the LORD.” Governor, priest, and remnant, the whole addressed audience of chapter 1, obeyed. There is no recorded debate, no committee, no second oracle needed to persuade them. The prophets before the exile had preached to kings who stopped their ears for decades. Haggai preached one sermon about a pierced bag, and the people feared the LORD.

What heaven sent back down the same channel was three words long. “Haggai, the messenger of the LORD, delivered the message of the LORD to the people,” and the message in full is this: “I am with you,” declares the LORD. The drought chapter ends on a summons; the answer to obedience is a presence. The book gives Haggai his title in this verse and nowhere else, the messenger of the LORD, and the one message he is introduced carrying is not a command at all. Consider carefully your ways had been the word for their hands. I am with you is the word for everything else.

The obedience still had to become lumber, and the text is precise about whose act that was. “So the LORD stirred the spirit of Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah, and the spirit of Joshua son of Jehozadak, the high priest, as well as the spirit of all the remnant of the people.” Stirred is the Bible's word for what God does to Cyrus in Ezra's telling, waking a man to a work prepared for him, and here it falls on a governor, a priest, and a remnant at once, in that order. They obeyed the voice; God stirred the spirits; the book keeps both verbs standing and does not merge them.

“And they came and began the work on the house of the LORD of Hosts, their God, on the twenty-fourth day of the sixth month, in the second year of King Darius.” Twenty-three days after the word arrived, the work began. The oracle had demanded they consider carefully, and the considering took three weeks, and then hands were on timber. Sixteen years of the time has not yet come were ended by a date the book is as careful to print as the date of the rebuke itself.

The episode is the shortest movement in the book, five verses between two oracles, and it is the hinge the whole story swings on. A ruined house, a busy people, a summoned drought: that was the first day of the sixth month. By the twenty-fourth day there were workers on the site and a presence promised over the work. What the builders would feel a month later, looking at how small the new walls stood against their memories of the old ones, is the next word heaven had for them, and it begins with a question for the oldest people on the site.

title: The Latter Glory of This House
subtitle: Haggai 2
description: The old men remember Solomon's glory; heaven answers with a shaking and a greater glory to come.
paragraphs: The work was not a month old when the second word came, dated like the first: on the twenty-first day of the seventh month, through Haggai, to the same governor, priest, and remnant. This oracle is not aimed at their hands. It is aimed at their eyes, and it opens by finding the oldest people on the building site and asking them the question that had clearly been going around the work crews: “Who is left among you who saw this house in its former glory? How does it look to you now? Does it not appear to you like nothing in comparison?” Solomon's temple had stood within living memory, barely. Men and women in their seventies had been children in its courts. Against that memory the new foundation's first courses looked like nothing, and heaven, instead of rebuking the comparison, asks it out loud.

The answer is a triple command addressed down the same chain as the obedience: “But now be strong, O Zerubbabel, declares the LORD. Be strong, O Joshua son of Jehozadak, the high priest. And be strong, all you people of the land, declares the LORD. Work! For I am with you, declares the LORD of Hosts.” The three-word message of the sixth month returns as the ground of the command, and then the oracle reaches back past the exile, past the monarchy, to the oldest promise the nation owned: “This is the promise I made to you when you came out of Egypt. And My Spirit remains among you; do not be afraid.” The same presence that came out of Egypt with them is standing in the half-built house in Jerusalem, and the builders are told to measure the work by that, not by their grandfathers' memories.

Then the oracle widens past the building site altogether. “Once more, in a little while, I will shake the heavens and the earth, the sea and the dry land. I will shake all the nations, and they will come with all their treasures, and I will fill this house with glory, says the LORD of Hosts.” The shaking that summoned a drought on one people's fields in chapter 1 is promised again at the scale of the nations, and this time what it shakes loose is treasure, flowing toward the little house whose poverty had just been measured against Solomon's. The ground of it is ownership, stated flatly: “The silver is Mine, and the gold is Mine, declares the LORD of Hosts.”

The promise lands in the sentence the book is remembered by: “The latter glory of this house will be greater than the former, says the LORD of Hosts. And in this place I will provide peace, declares the LORD of Hosts.” Greater, not equal, not restored-to-former. The old men comparing courses of stone are answered with a future they will not live to measure, attached to the very house their hands are building, and sealed with the provision of peace in this place. The oracle does not tell them how the latter glory will outrun the former, or when the shaking comes. It tells them to work, on the strength of a presence and a promise, and it leaves the arithmetic of glory to God.

Two months later, on a single day, the word would come twice more, and the second of those two messages would reach past the builders to the governor alone, and past the temple to the thrones of the nations. But first there was a question for the priests, and it was about how defilement travels.

title: From This Day On, I Will Bless You
subtitle: Haggai 2
description: A ruling from the priests, a blessing dated over bare branches, and a signet ring restored.
paragraphs: On the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month, three months into the work, the word came to Haggai with an assignment for the priests: “Ask the priests for a ruling.” The question was about consecrated meat carried in the fold of a garment. If the garment touches bread, stew, wine, oil, or any other food, does that food become holy? The priests answered no, holiness does not travel by contact. Then the second question: “If one who is defiled by contact with a corpse touches any of these, does it become defiled?” “Yes, it becomes defiled,” the priests answered. Defilement travels. Holiness does not. The ruling is the parable, and Haggai turns it on the nation without pausing: “So it is with this people and this nation before Me, declares the LORD, and so it is with every work of their hands; whatever they offer there is defiled.” Years of offerings at a ruined house had not sanctified the offerers. The uncleanness had been spreading through everything their hands produced.

Which is why the fields had been preaching the same sermon as the prophet. “Now consider carefully from this day forward,” the oracle runs, the book's refrain turned toward the calendar: “Before one stone was placed on another in the temple of the LORD,” when a man came expecting a heap of twenty ephahs of grain, there were but ten, and at the winepress, drawing for fifty baths, there were but twenty. Half harvests, exactly half, the pierced bag measured out in produce. God states His own hand in it in fragments around the sentence's hard center: “I struck you,” He says, “all the work of your hands,” “with blight, mildew, and hail, but you did not turn to Me, declares the LORD.”

Then the refrain comes a final time, with the date underlined twice over: “Consider carefully from this day forward,” from “the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month, the day the foundation of the LORD’s temple was laid,” consider carefully. And the blessing is pronounced over a landscape that gives it no evidence at all: “Is there still seed in the barn? The vine, the fig, the pomegranate, and the olive tree have not yet yielded fruit. But from this day on, I will bless you.” The barn is empty, the trees are bare, winter is on the land, and the blessing is dated anyway, from this day, the day of the foundation, not from the day the first crop proves it. The book's whole arithmetic reverses in that sentence: the lean years were reckoned backward from the ruin, and the blessed years will be reckoned forward from the foundation.

The same day, the word came a second time, for one man. “Tell Zerubbabel governor of Judah that I am about to shake the heavens and the earth,” and the shaking this time is thrones: “I will overturn royal thrones and destroy the power of the kingdoms of the nations. I will overturn chariots and their riders; horses and their riders will fall, each by the sword of his brother.”

Then, to the governor who had been handed lumber and a work order and a triple be strong, comes the book's last word: “On that day, declares the LORD of Hosts, I will take you, My servant, Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, declares the LORD, and I will make you like My signet ring, for I have chosen you, declares the LORD of Hosts.” A signet ring is the seal a king presses into clay to sign his decrees, the most personal object he owns. In Jeremiah's book, already told in this series, God had torn a signet ring off this man's grandfather Jehoiachin and sworn he would prosper no more in the land. Here the grandson is named the ring on God's own hand, chosen. Haggai ends there, the blessing spoken over bare branches and the promise spoken over a governor, neither of them yet visible, both of them dated.
